pages.name: The same step, again
pages.text: Some changes repeat, like a pump that runs every hour. Doing a matrix step n times means working out `Aⁿ`. With no steps nothing moves, so the card starts at `A⁰ = [1 0; 0 1]`. Each step moves the flag by `A = [3 1; 0 2]`, so it leans and grows. The card reads `A² = [9 5; 0 4]`, then `A³ = [27 19; 0 8]`. Each is a full multiplication, which is slow and hides where the steps head.

pages.name: Four steps along (1, 0)
pages.task: `(1, 0)` is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue 3. Where is it after four steps?
pages.why: An eigenvector is only stretched. Each step multiplies `(1, 0)` by 3 again. So four steps multiply it by `3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81`. That gives `(81, 0)`, still on the same line.

pages.name: Measure along the eigenvectors
pages.text: The eigenvector grid runs along `(1, 0)`, with eigenvalue 3, and `(−1, 1)`, with eigenvalue 2. A basis of eigenvectors, an [[eigenbasis]], reads the flag as amounts of each. A acts on each part separately, so `A(a(1, 0) + b(−1, 1))` `= 3a(1, 0) + 2b(−1, 1)`. So each step multiplies the first amount by 3 and the second by 2. The second card climbs from `D⁰ = [1 0; 0 1]` to `D³ = [27 0; 0 8]`. D is a [[diagonal matrix]].

pages.name: Amounts after three steps
pages.task: The arrow `(1, 1)` is 2 lots of `(1, 0)` plus 1 lot of `(−1, 1)`. So its amounts are `(2, 1)`. What are they after three steps?
pages.why: Each step multiplies the first amount by 3 and the second by 2. Three steps multiply them by `3³ = 27` and `2³ = 8`. So the amounts are `2 × 27 = 54` and `1 × 8 = 8`. Back on the square grid that is `54(1, 0) + 8(−1, 1)`, which is `(46, 8)`.

pages.name: Into the grid and out again
pages.text: Put the eigenvectors in as the columns of `P = [1 −1; 0 1]`. P turns amounts on the eigenvector grid into your numbers. `P⁻¹ = [1 1; 0 1]` turns your numbers into amounts. So `A = PDP⁻¹`. Read it right to left. P⁻¹ turns `(1, 1)` into the amounts `(2, 1)`. D stretches them to `(6, 2)`. P turns that back into `(4, 2)`, which is `A(1, 1)`. To [[diagonalise]] A is to find this P and D. Three-phase fault studies use the same move, called symmetrical components.

pages.name: Swap P’s columns
pages.task: Take P’s columns the other way round, `(−1, 1)` first and `(1, 0)` second. What is D now?
pages.why: Each eigenvalue sits in the column of its own eigenvector. Column 1 is now `(−1, 1)`, which A stretches by 2. Column 2 is `(1, 0)`, which A stretches by 3. So `D = [2 0; 0 3]`. Swapping P’s columns swaps D’s entries.

pages.name: Many steps at once
pages.text: Now repeat it. `A³` is `PDP⁻¹` three times over. Each `P⁻¹P` in the middle is I, which changes nothing. So `A³ = PD³P⁻¹`. In general `Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹`. Dⁿ just raises each diagonal entry to the power n. Here `PDⁿ = [3ⁿ −2ⁿ; 0 2ⁿ]`. Multiplying by `P⁻¹ = [1 1; 0 1]` gives `Aⁿ = [3ⁿ 3ⁿ − 2ⁿ; 0 2ⁿ]`. So `A¹⁰ =` `[59049 58025; 0 1024]`, with no long multiplying.

pages.task: Someone works out `A³` as `PDP⁻¹` and gets `[3 1; 0 2]`. What went wrong?

pages.name: Where the steps head
pages.text: Each hour a pump moves 20% of tank 1’s water to tank 2, and 30% of tank 2’s back. So `A = [0.8 0.3; 0.2 0.7]`. `A(3, 2) = (3, 2)` and `A(1, −1) = (0.5, −0.5)`, so its eigenvalues are 1 and 0.5. The start `(1000, 0)` is `200(3, 2) + 400(1, −1)`. Each hour the first part stays and the second halves. So the water heads for `200(3, 2) = (600, 400)`, a 60 : 40 split.

pages.name: Too few eigenvectors
pages.text: Not every matrix can be diagonalised. It needs one independent eigenvector for each column. The shear `[1 1; 0 1]` has `det(A − λI) = (1 − λ)²`, so λ = 1 twice. But `A − I = [0 1; 0 0]` crushes only the line through `(1, 0)`. One line makes no grid, so there is no P. λ = 1 has [[algebraic multiplicity]] 2 but [[geometric multiplicity]] 1. `2I` has λ = 2 twice, yet every line is an eigenvector line.

pages.task: `M = [0.7 0.2; 0.2 0.7]` stretches `(1, 1)` by 0.9 and `(1, −1)` by 0.5. Start at `(1, 0)`, which is half of each, and take 20 steps. Which line is the arrow nearly on?
pages.why: Each part is multiplied by its own eigenvalue every step. After 20 steps the `(1, 1)` part is `0.5 × 0.9²⁰`, about 0.06. The `(1, −1)` part is `0.5 × 0.5²⁰`, less than a millionth. So the part with the bigger eigenvalue takes over.
